A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–H and adds Appendices I–J.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting and control experiments on Van der Pol, Lorenz, Rössler and weather data, including numerical results and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds household-voltage and bicycle-count forecasting experiments, component ablations and sensitivity studies.

M1.justification: The sampling construction, EDMD fitting, recurrent architecture and prediction/control procedures in Algorithms 1–4 remain unchanged. Appendix J evaluates component-removal variants without changing the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix I substantially broadens the real-world coverage beyond Jena weather by adding household-voltage forecasting using the individual power consumption dataset and bicycle-count forecasting in Copenhagen. All original synthetic, partially observed, controlled and weather tasks remain.

E2.justification: The original ESN, shPLRNN and LSTM comparisons retain their comparator membership. Appendix J adds Gaussian-weight/uniform-bias sampling with EDMD and direct-map alternatives without EDMD, evaluated with and without SWIM in Table 8 and Figure 17.

E3.justification: The original benchmark protocols remain unchanged. New experiments introduce a 4–512-neuron sweep, a Van der Pol time-step sweep from 0.1 to 0.5, and forecasting protocols for voltage and bicycle counts. Voltage uses a two/one/one-week split and four-hour context/two-hour horizon; bicycle forecasting uses fourteen-hour context/seven-hour horizon.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s existing Van der Pol width/runtime analyses, v2 adds chaotic-system width sensitivity in Figure 11, separate SWIM and Koopman component ablations in Table 8, and time-step sensitivity with and without Koopman lifting in Figure 17. These substantially expand evidence about component contributions and robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-seed replication and mean/minimum/maximum reporting. The new chaotic-width study explicitly uses five runs, and the component comparisons retain the existing uncertainty format. No increased run count, new uncertainty estimator or significance test is reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the retained figure results are unchanged, but v2 adds substantial new results. Appendix I reports test MSEs of 1.428 for voltage and 140 for bicycle counts. Table 8 adds component-comparison scores, while Figures 11 and 17 add width and time-step trends; these are additional results, not improvements over v1 under revised settings.

T1.justification: Appendix A, Equation (10), corrects repeated composition of K applied to an observable into repeated composition of the Koopman operator followed by application to the observable. The convergence theorems, assumptions and proofs otherwise retain their mathematical substance.

C1.justification: The abstract and central gradient-free training and convergence claims remain intact. The revised introduction makes the contribution claims more specific by explicitly attributing an additional performance benefit to Koopman lifting beyond SWIM sampling.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new ablations as evidence for combining SWIM and Koopman lifting and discusses greater consistency as prediction time steps increase. Appendix H identifies possible Rössler overfitting, and the conclusion makes the difficulty with high-dimensional data explicit.

D1.justification: Appendices I–J add dataset sources, preprocessing and time embeddings, forecasting windows, hidden-layer sizes, activations and ablation sampling distributions. Appendix I identifies the previously specified hardware used. Existing implementation information, hyperparameter tables and code access links remain.

R1.justification: V2 removes the Gallos et al. (2024) and Galaris et al. (2022) citations, adds sources for the two new datasets, and relates the time-step findings to Mauroy and Goncalves (2017). The broader positioning against reservoir computing and prior Koopman methods remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction is locally rewritten to foreground two contributions, dictionary notation is simplified, and several passages are shortened or edited. Appendices I–J extend the document, while the existing section organization and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds a substantial suite of visual evidence: chaotic-width plots, dataset splits and forecasts, time-step comparisons, and Table 8. These appear in six new figures, numbered 11 and 13–17. V1’s Figure 11 becomes Figure 12; existing figures and tables also shift position without changing their underlying results.

improvement.justification: Table 8 and Figures 11 and 17 strengthen the justification for combining SWIM with Koopman lifting and clarify sensitivity to width and prediction time step. Equation (10) is also corrected. The added real-world examples broaden illustration but lack baseline comparisons, limiting their comparative value. These gains improve an already empirically supported paper while leaving its central method and main benchmark evidence unchanged.
